body.text: These two are constantly confused, and one comparison separates them: **whose cost is the price below?**

**Predatory pricing** sets a price below the SELLER's own average variable cost, held long enough to drive a rival out, then raised. Chapter 4's incumbent has an average cost of $20 a unit and average variable cost $16. A predatory $14 loses $2 a unit on the variable costs alone — below chapter 2's shutdown point, which no firm accepts except for what it does to a rival. If the rival leaves and the price goes to $34, it recovers $14 a unit.

**Limit pricing** sets a price below an ENTRANT's average cost and above the seller's own: $28, against $32 and $20. The incumbent profits by $8 a unit throughout — sacrificing some profit and never making a loss.

So predatory pricing is a deliberate loss to remove a rival; limit pricing is a reduced profit taken indefinitely to stop one arriving. Predatory pricing is unlawful in most jurisdictions as an abuse of dominance; limit pricing is hard to tell from competitive pricing.
Both only pay if the price can be raised afterwards, so both depend on chapter 4's barriers. Where entry is easy, a predator that clears the market meets a new entrant the moment the price goes up.

realExample.text: A bus operator running a competing service at a fare below its own fuel and wage cost is pricing predatorily. One holding a fare a newcomer could not match while covering its own costs is limit pricing.

sections.misconception: Students call any very low price predatory. The test is the seller's own average variable cost: above it the firm is competing, below it it is paying to remove a rival.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Explain of a reason as including analysis, since it needs a two-stage chain: which cost the price sits below, and what that implies about whether the seller is losing money.

recall.prompt: An incumbent has an average cost of $20 and an average variable cost of $16; an entrant would face $32. Name each of these three prices:
template: $28 is a ___ price: it blocks entry and the incumbent still profits
$14 is a ___ price: it is under the seller's own avoidable cost
$38 is neither, because it is above what an ___ would have to cover and entry would pay
hints: the price that stops a rival arriving
the price that removes a rival already there
whose cost decides whether entry pays

sections.title: Non-Price Competition: Five Forms
sections.keyIdea: Where a price cut will be matched within days, firms compete by advertising and branding, quality, endorsement, product placement and after-sales service instead.

body.text: In an oligopoly a price cut is visible and matched by the afternoon, and chapter 5 showed where matching leads. **Non-price competition** is what firms do instead — the normal state of most oligopolies, not the exception.
The specification names five forms.

items: **Advertising and branding** — spending that makes buyers ask for this firm’s product by name rather than compare prices.
**Quality** — a product that lasts longer or works better, which wins buyers without a price cut.
**Endorsement** — a person or body buyers already trust is associated with the product.
**Product placement** — the product is shown in a setting buyers are already watching rather than in an advertisement.
**After-sales service** — servicing, warranties and support that make the purchase less risky.

body.text: Why firms prefer it. A price cut is **immediately matched** and leaves everybody with the same customers and less money. A reputation for quality or a service network takes rivals **years** to copy, so the advantage lasts — and it makes the firm's demand curve less elastic, which is worth more than one season's sales.

And it is safer. A price cut invites retaliation in the same currency; a campaign invites a rival campaign, costing both money without lowering either price. Interdependence still operates, on a battleground where the firms keep their margins.

realExample.text: Mobile networks in one country usually charge near-identical tariffs while competing on handset bundles, network coverage claims, sponsorships and the speed at which a fault is fixed.

sections.misconception: Students list non-price competition as advertising and brand loyalty only. The specification names five forms and three of them are easy to forget: endorsement, product placement and after-sales service. Instead: learn all five, because a question can name any of them.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Define as requiring the meaning of a term, concept or phrase. Non-price competition is any attempt to win customers other than by lowering price — and the examples do not substitute for saying so.

recall.prompt: Match each activity to the form of non-price competition it is:

pairs.left: A three-year warranty and a repair network
pairs.right: After-sales service
pairs.why: Servicing, warranties and support after the sale reduce the buyer’s risk, which is after-sales service.

pairs.left: A well-known athlete associated with the product
pairs.right: Endorsement
pairs.why: A person or body buyers already trust being associated with the product is endorsement.

pairs.left: The product visible in a popular programme
pairs.right: Product placement
pairs.why: Showing the product in a setting buyers are already watching, rather than in an advertisement, is product placement.

pairs.left: A component that lasts twice as long at the same price
pairs.right: Quality
pairs.why: A product that works better or lasts longer wins buyers without a price cut, which is competing on quality.

sections.title: Costs and Benefits of Price and Non-Price Competition
sections.keyIdea: Price competition moves money to consumers and squeezes firms; non-price competition raises costs and can improve the product.

body.text: The specification asks for costs and benefits of price AND non-price competition to four groups: **firms, consumers, employees and suppliers** — a different list from chapter 5's collusion leaf, which named workers and governments.

**Firms.** Price competition lowers margins and can end a firm, and forces out X-inefficiency, since a firm that cannot cut cost cannot survive the price. Non-price competition protects the margin and raises fixed costs — a budget and a service network are owed whether sales rise or not — which itself becomes a barrier to entry.

**Consumers.** Price competition is a gain while it lasts: lower price, more bought. Non-price competition brings better products, more choice and more information, at the cost of paying for the advertising in the price — and some of it is persuasion rather than information.

**Employees.** Non-price competition means more secure employment and skilled work in design, marketing and service. Price competition pressures wages and staffing, though it can expand employment where the lower price wins a larger market.

**Suppliers.** A firm squeezed on price passes the squeeze up the chain: hard on suppliers, and it can lower costs across the industry. A firm competing on quality needs reliable inputs and long relationships, which suits a supplier that can deliver them and shuts out one that cannot.

realExample.text: Grocery chains fighting on price press their growers on cost; the same chains competing on freshness pay more and sign longer contracts.

sections.misconception: Students judge the two kinds of competition as good and bad. Each has a cost and a benefit for all four groups, and the best answers are where the two pull one group in opposite directions — as they do for employees and suppliers.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 says Examine requires evaluation and a brief assessment of the arguments as well as a chain of reasoning, focusing on depth rather than breadth. Two groups taken properly will do more than four listed.

recall.prompt: Sort each effect by whether it comes from price competition or from non-price competition:

groups.name: Price competition
items: A grocery chain presses its growers for another two per cent
The weakest firm in the market closes after two thin years
A depot finally removes the overtime it could not justify
groups.why: Everything here follows from the price itself falling: thinner margins, cost pressure inside the firm and pressure passed to suppliers.

groups.name: Non-price competition
items: A firm takes on designers and a sponsorship budget it must pay for every year
A three-year warranty and a repair network the buyer funds in the price
A new entrant finds it must outspend an established name before selling anything
groups.why: Everything here follows from spending to win customers some other way: the spending is a fixed cost, it creates work, and buyers fund it.

takeaway: A price war is matched cuts: good for consumers, and it can concentrate the market.
Predatory is below the SELLER's own AVC, a deliberate loss; limit pricing is below an ENTRANT's AC.
Five forms: advertising and branding, quality, endorsement, placement, after-sales service.
Costs and benefits to FIRMS, CONSUMERS, EMPLOYEES and SUPPLIERS — a different list from collusion’s.

content.title: Monopoly

sections.title: Assumptions and Barriers
sections.keyIdea: A pure monopoly is the only seller of a product with no close substitute, protected by barriers high enough to keep it the only seller.

body.text: **Monopoly** is the other extreme from chapter 2. One seller, no close substitute, and barriers to entry high enough that the position holds.

items: **A single seller** of the product, so the firm's demand curve IS the market demand curve.
**No close substitutes**, so buyers who want the product have no alternative supplier.
**High barriers to entry and exit**, which is what preserves the position — the six of chapter 4, at their strongest.
**Profit maximisation** at MR = MC, as everywhere else in this section.
**Price setting**: the firm chooses its price, and the quantity it sells follows from the demand curve.

body.text: The **barriers** deserve naming rather than assuming, because they decide whether the position is temporary or permanent. A patent monopoly expires. A monopoly resting on economies of scale — chapter 7's natural monopoly — lasts as long as the technology does. A legal monopoly lasts as long as the law. A monopoly held only by branding is the most fragile of the four.

In practice competition law defines a dominant position at a share well below 100%, because a firm with most of a market and no effective rival behaves much as a pure monopolist does. The model is the extreme case; its predictions apply in weaker form to firms with market power short of it.

realExample.text: A city's metro system is the only supplier of its service within its network, protected by a construction cost nobody would repeat and by the law under which it operates.

sections.misconception: Students require a 100% share before calling a firm a monopolist, then conclude the model applies to almost nothing. The assumptions are an extreme case; a firm with substantial market power and no close substitute behaves in the same direction.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Explain of the characteristics as requiring knowledge, understanding and application. The application is that a single seller faces the MARKET demand curve, which is what gives it a choice of price at all.

recall.prompt: A city metro is the only supplier of its service and no one may build a second. Complete what follows:
template: The demand curve this firm faces is the whole ___ demand curve, so it slopes downward
It can therefore choose its ___, and the quantity it sells follows from the curve
What keeps the position is the construction cost and the law, which are ___ to entry
hints: whose demand curve a single seller ends up facing
the variable a single seller gets to set
the general name for what keeps rivals out

sections.title: Profit-Maximising Equilibrium
sections.keyIdea: The monopolist produces where MR = MC and prices off the demand curve above that output, so price exceeds marginal cost and supernormal profit can persist.

body.text: Zahra Water is the only supplier of piped water in its area. Its demand curve is **P = 120 − 4Q**, in dollars a megalitre, so marginal revenue is **MR = 120 − 8Q**. Marginal cost is $24 a megalitre at every output.
Profit is maximised where **MR = MC**: 120 − 8Q = 24 gives **Q = 12 megalitres a day**.

The price comes from the **demand curve** at that output, not from the marginal revenue curve: P = 120 − 4 × 12 = **$72**. Profit is ($72 − $24) × 12 = **$576** a day, and unlike chapters 2 and 3 there is no entry to compete it away.

Compare that with what a competitive industry with the same costs would do. Competition drives price to marginal cost, so P = $24 and, from the demand curve, Q = 24 megalitres. The monopolist produces **12 megalitres less** and charges **$48 more**.

Notice that the monopolist does not charge the highest price it can. At $72 it sells 12 megalitres; it could charge more and sell fewer. The demand curve constrains it, and MR = MC identifies the most profitable point on that curve.

realExample.text: A water network supplies less at a higher price than a competitive industry with the same pipes and pumps would, which is why such networks are usually regulated on price rather than left alone.

sections.misconception: Students say a monopolist "can charge what it likes" or reads the price off the MR curve. It faces a downward-sloping demand curve, so a higher price means fewer sales; and the price is read off AR above the MR = MC output.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Draw as requiring an accurately labelled diagram using quantitative skills. The labels that carry the marks are the output where MR cuts MC, the price vertically above it ON the demand curve, and the profit area between price and average cost.

recall.prompt: Complete the monopoly equilibrium for a demand curve P = 120 − 4Q with marginal cost $24:
template: Marginal revenue is 120 − ___Q, twice as steep as AR
Setting marginal revenue equal to marginal cost gives an output of ___ megalitres
The price is read off the ___ curve above that output, giving $72
hints: double the gradient of the demand curve
solve the equation for Q
the curve that says what buyers will pay

sections.title: Costs and Benefits to Firms and Consumers
sections.keyIdea: Consumers pay more and get less, and their loss exceeds the firm's gain by the welfare loss — but scale and innovation are real arguments the other way.

body.text: The specification asks for costs and benefits to **firms and consumers**, and the previous subsection's arithmetic measures most of it.

**Consumers pay the cost.** Price rises from $24 to $72, quantity falls from 24 to 12 megalitres, and consumer surplus falls from $1,152 to $288. Part is **transferred** to the firm as profit of $576; the rest goes nowhere.

**The welfare loss** is that remainder: the triangle between demand and marginal cost over the 12 megalitres not produced, with area ½ × 12 × $48 = **$288** a day. Those megalitres were worth more to buyers than they would have cost to supply.

**The firm gains** $576, and more than money: security, the ability to plan, research funded from retained profit. There is also a case that the prize of a monopoly position motivates the innovation that creates one.

**The arguments the other way.** A monopolist's scale may bring average cost BELOW what many small firms could reach, so the price may be lower than a competitive industry could offer — the next subsection's natural monopoly. And supernormal profit is where dynamic efficiency is funded, so a higher price now may buy a better product later. Neither is automatic: a monopolist MAY pass on scale economies and MAY invest, or may let X-inefficiency grow.

realExample.text: A single electricity network can be cheaper per household than competing sets of cables, and has no reason to pass the saving on unless a regulator requires it.

sections.misconception: Students assert that monopoly always harms consumers. The static case is strong and the scale and innovation arguments are real; what keeps them arguments is that the firm need not pass anything on.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 says Evaluate requires multi-stage chains of reasoning and a critical assessment so that informed judgements may be made. The judgement here rests on whether the scale and innovation arguments hold in the particular market.

recall.prompt: Complete the welfare arithmetic for this monopolist against a competitive industry with the same costs:
template: The monopolist produces 12 megalitres at $72, against a competitive 24 at $24, so it ___ 12 megalitres
Its profit of $576 is ___ from consumers rather than lost
The welfare loss of $288 goes to ___
hints: what the firm does with the output it does not make
what happens to the money the firm gains
who ends up with the remainder

sections.title: Natural Monopoly
sections.keyIdea: Where average cost falls across the whole range of market demand, one firm supplies more cheaply than several — so competition itself raises costs.

body.text: A **natural monopoly** exists where long-run average cost falls **continuously** across the whole range of market demand: minimum efficient scale is as large as the market or larger, so there is no room for two firms at an efficient size.
The arithmetic is one division. Say the network costs $9,000 a day whatever it carries, plus $2 a unit delivered: average cost is $2 + $9,000 ÷ Q, falling at every output and never turning up.

The market takes 1,000 units a day. **One firm** supplies all of them at $11 a unit. **Two firms** supply 500 each at $20, each duplicating the whole network for half the customers. Competition has raised the cost of supply by $9 a unit, $9,000 a day, for nothing.

**The implications** are what the specification asks for. Competition is wasteful here, so the usual remedy does not apply — but a natural monopoly left alone still restricts output and raises price, because the cost advantage does not remove the incentive. So policy usually allows one supplier and **regulates** it: cap the price, require a service standard, or own it publicly.
And the boundary moves with technology: a network monopoly stops being natural when something serves the same need without the network, which is why the list is shorter than it was.

realExample.text: Two sets of water mains down one street would double the buried cost and deliver the same water — which is why water networks are single suppliers almost everywhere, and regulated.

sections.misconception: Students call any large monopoly natural. The test is whether average cost is still falling at the size of the whole market: a firm with a flat average cost curve over that range is not one, however large.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 says Analyse requires a chain of reasoning and diagrams where appropriate, focusing on depth rather than breadth. The chain is continuously falling average cost, then the cost of splitting output between two firms, then the conclusion about competition.

recall.prompt: Complete the natural-monopoly case and what follows for policy:
template: A natural monopoly exists where long-run average cost is still ___ at an output as large as the whole market
One firm serving 1,000 units has an average cost of $11; two firms serving half each have $20, so competition ___ the cost of supply
A natural monopoly left alone still restricts output, so the usual policy answer is to allow one supplier and ___ it
hints: which way the curve is still going at that output
what splitting the market does to cost per unit
what to do instead of breaking it up

sections.title: Conditions for Third-Degree Price Discrimination
sections.keyIdea: Charging different prices to different groups for the same product needs market power, separable groups with different elasticities, and no resale between them.

body.text: **Third-degree price discrimination** is charging different GROUPS different prices for the same product, where the difference does not reflect a difference in cost. The specification asks for the conditions necessary, and there are three.
**One: market power.** The firm must be able to set its price. A perfectly competitive grower cannot charge two prices, because it cannot charge a price at all.

**Two: separable groups with different price elasticities of demand.** The firm must know which group a buyer is in, and the groups must differ in price sensitivity. Different elasticities are what make two prices more profitable than one: the group that will not switch pays more.

**Three: no resale between the groups.** If the cheap group can sell on to the expensive group, the two prices collapse into one and the arrangement is worth nothing to the firm. This is why discrimination is common in services — a haircut or a bus ride cannot be resold — and difficult in portable goods.

Groups are separated by whatever the firm can verify and the buyer cannot fake: age, student or resident status, time of day, how far ahead a booking is made, household or business. Separating and enforcing costs money, and it must cost less than the extra profit.

realExample.text: A theatre charges students less for the same seat, checks a card at the door, and loses nothing by it: the seat cannot be resold and the students would not have come at the full price.

sections.misconception: Students call any price difference discrimination. A peak fare reflecting a higher cost of supplying at peak is not; discrimination is a different price for the SAME product at the same cost. Check the cost first.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Explain of a term or the characteristics as requiring knowledge, understanding and application. Applying the conditions means saying why each is necessary — particularly the no-resale condition, which is the one students name without explaining.

recall.prompt: Complete the three conditions necessary for third-degree price discrimination:
template: The firm must have market ___, so that it can set a price at all
The groups must be separable and must differ in their price ___ of demand
And there must be no ___ between the groups, or the two prices collapse into one
hints: what a firm facing a horizontal demand curve does not have
the property that makes two prices pay better than one
what the cheap group must not be able to do

sections.title: Costs and Benefits of Price Discrimination
sections.keyIdea: The firm charges each group what it will bear; some consumers pay more and some are served at all, so the verdict depends which group you are in.

body.text: Zahra Water sells the same piped water into two markets it can tell apart and between which nothing can be resold. Marginal cost is $24 a megalitre in both.

**Market A** is business users with no alternative supply: P = 120 − 4Q. MR = MC gives 12 megalitres at **$72**, elasticity −1.50. **Market B** is households who can store or go without: P = 72 − 1.5Q, giving 16 megalitres at **$48**, elasticity −2.00.

There is the rule, and it falls out of the arithmetic rather than being asserted: **the less elastic market pays the higher price.** $24 more, for the same piped water at the same cost. Total profit is $960.

**For the firm** the benefit is that profit, each group charged closer to what it will bear. Against it: separating the groups, policing resale, and the regulatory risk if buyers think the difference unfair.

**For consumers** there is no single answer. The inelastic group pays more. The elastic group pays less than a single price would be — and in some markets is served only because of discrimination, since one price might be set above what it would pay. The profit can also cover fixed costs a single price would not, which is the argument for discriminatory fares on a route that would otherwise close.

realExample.text: A rail operator charges a commuter with no alternative more than an off-peak traveller who could stay at home, for the same seat.

sections.misconception: Students say price discrimination is unfair and therefore harmful. Some pay more, some pay less, and some are served who would not be at a single price — so the verdict depends on which group is asked.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 says Discuss requires a recognition of different viewpoints and a critical assessment of the evidence. Here two groups of consumers have opposite experiences of one policy, which is why "consumers lose" cannot be the answer.

recall.prompt: Match each party to what third-degree price discrimination does to it:

pairs.left: Buyers whose demand is less elastic
pairs.right: Pay the higher price, $72 here
pairs.why: The group that will not switch is the one that can be charged more, which is why different elasticities are a necessary condition.

pairs.left: Buyers whose demand is more elastic
pairs.right: Pay less than a single price would be, $48 here
pairs.why: Charging the switchers less is what wins their custom, so discrimination is not simply a loss to every consumer.

pairs.right: Raises profit, and pays to separate the groups and police resale
pairs.why: Each group is charged closer to what it will bear, and the separating and enforcing is the cost of doing so.

pairs.left: A group a single price would have excluded
pairs.right: Is served at all, where one price would have been set above what it would pay
pairs.why: This is the strongest argument for discrimination: without it a firm setting one price might have left that group unserved.

sections.title: Productive, Allocative and Dynamic Efficiency
sections.keyIdea: A monopoly fails the two static efficiency tests and may pass the dynamic one, which is the whole of the argument about whether it should be broken up.

body.text: All three tests, and the answers mirror chapter 2's.

**Allocative efficiency: no.** P is $72 and MC is $24, so too little is produced — 12 megalitres too little, a welfare cost of $288 a day. The failure is unavoidable: a profit maximiser sets MR = MC, and MR is below AR, so P exceeds MC necessarily.

**Productive efficiency: no reason to expect it.** Nothing drives the monopolist to the bottom of its average cost curve, because it does not need the lowest cost to survive — and the absence of pressure is the classic setting for **X-inefficiency**.

**Dynamic efficiency: possibly, and this is the real argument.** Supernormal profit of $576 a day can fund research a firm on normal profit could not, and protection from imitation lets it capture the return. Against that, a firm with no rival has less need to innovate.

So the case against monopoly is static and measurable and the case for it dynamic and conditional. That asymmetry is why policy rarely breaks a monopoly up and instead attacks the conditions: regulate the price, require network access, remove the legal barrier, or — as chapter 8 shows — make entry credible enough that the firm behaves as if it had a rival.

realExample.text: A patent lets a developer price well above manufacturing cost: allocatively inefficient, and also what repaid the development. When it expires, price falls towards cost and the incentive to develop the next one goes with it.

sections.misconception: Students conclude that monopoly is inefficient and should be broken up. It fails two tests, may pass the third, and where it is a natural monopoly breaking it up raises costs.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 says Evaluate requires the validity and significance of arguments to be considered and supported by chains of reasoning, with a critical assessment so that informed judgements may be made. Weighing a measurable static loss against a conditional dynamic gain is that judgement.

recall.prompt: Sort each efficiency test by what a profit-maximising monopoly does on it:

groups.name: Fails necessarily
items: Allocative efficiency, because MR lies below AR so price exceeds marginal cost
groups.why: This one is not a tendency but an implication: a profit maximiser sets MR = MC, and MR is below AR, so P is above MC whatever the firm intends.

groups.name: No pressure towards it
items: Productive efficiency, since the firm need not reach the lowest cost to survive
Freedom from X-inefficiency, since nothing forces costs down
groups.why: Neither is impossible; there is simply nothing in the structure that drives the firm towards them, which is the classic setting for costs drifting upward.

groups.name: May be delivered
items: Dynamic efficiency, funded from supernormal profit
Innovation whose return the firm can capture because imitation is blocked
groups.why: Supernormal profit and protection from imitation are exactly what a long research programme needs — which is why the case for monopoly is dynamic and conditional.

takeaway: One seller, no close substitute, high barriers. The firm’s demand curve IS the market demand curve.
MR = MC gives 12 megalitres; the price comes off AR at $72; profit $576 and no entry to remove it.
Against a competitive $24 and 24 megalitres: 12 withheld and a welfare loss of $288.
Natural monopoly: one firm at $11 beats two at $20. Regulate, do not split.
Price discrimination needs power, DIFFERENT elasticities, no resale. The inelastic group pays more.
Fails allocative and productive efficiency; MAY deliver dynamic. That asymmetry is the argument.

content.title: Monopsony and Contestability

sections.title: Monopsony: a Single Buyer
sections.keyIdea: A monopsony is the only buyer, so the supply curve it faces is the average cost of what it buys — and the marginal cost rises twice as fast.

body.text: Every chapter so far has been about a seller with power. **Monopsony** is the mirror: a single **buyer** facing many sellers.

items: **One buyer**, or one dominant buyer, of the good or labour in question.
**Many sellers**, none able to go elsewhere — the condition that matters most.
**Barriers to other buyers entering**: legal, geographical or of scale.
**The buyer minimises its costs**, as a monopolist maximises revenue.

body.text: One step carries the rest. The **supply curve** of an input slopes up. For a single buyer it is the **average** cost of what it buys — and to get one more unit the price must rise for EVERY unit, not just the last. So the **marginal** cost of the input rises twice as fast.

Take the only cannery in a fishing town. Supply of workers is w = $20 + 2.5L, so the marginal cost of labour is $20 + 5L. It hires while that lies below the worker's **marginal revenue product**, here $200 − 5L.
Setting the two equal gives **18 workers**, and the wage comes off the SUPPLY curve there: **$65**. Note which curve — supply, not marginal cost — just as a monopolist's price comes off demand.

realExample.text: The only employer in a town faces workers who cannot take their labour elsewhere, and knows that offering more to hire one more means paying more to everyone.

sections.misconception: Students read the wage off the MCL curve, which gives too high a wage. MCL locates the EMPLOYMENT level; supply gives the wage that attracts that many workers. The condition is also written as "marginal cost equals marginal benefit"; it is the marginal cost of the input against its marginal revenue product.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Explain of a reason as including analysis, since it needs a two-stage chain: a single buyer must raise the price for every unit to get one more, so the marginal cost of the input lies above its supply curve.

recall.prompt: Put these in the order in which they follow as a single buyer decides what to pay:
correctOrder: Supply of the input slopes upward: more is offered at a higher price
Being the only buyer, the firm faces that curve as the AVERAGE cost of what it buys
To attract one more unit it must raise the price for every unit it already buys
So marginal cost rises twice as fast, and employment settles where it meets marginal revenue product at 18 workers
The wage is then read off the supply curve at that point: $65
why: An upward-sloping supply curve is the starting fact; everything else in the chain is a consequence of it.
It is being the ONLY buyer that turns the market supply curve into this firm’s average cost of the input.
This is the step students skip, and it is the one that separates the average from the marginal.
Twice the gradient follows from raising the price for every unit, and the quantity is settled by that marginal comparison.
The price comes last and off a DIFFERENT curve, which is the error the whole chain exists to prevent.

sections.title: Costs and Benefits of a Monopsony
sections.keyIdea: A monopsony buys less at a lower price than a competitive market would, which cuts its costs and leaves sellers worse off.

body.text: The specification asks for costs and benefits to **firms, consumers and employees**. Compare the outcome with a competitive market for the same input.

Competitively the wage settles where supply meets marginal revenue product: **24 workers at $80**. Under monopsony, **18 at $65** — 6 fewer jobs, $15 a worker less. The last worker adds $110 and is paid $65: a gap of $45.

**For the firm**: a lower input cost, higher profit, more control over its supply chain. Against it, a wage below what the work is worth makes recruitment harder, and a supplier squeezed to the edge may fail — leaving the buyer without a supply.

**For employees and other sellers**, mostly cost: a lower price and fewer selling. Hence the case for a minimum wage here — a floor between $65 and $80 raises BOTH wage and employment, which it could not do in a competitive market.

**For consumers** it depends what the buyer does with the saving. A monopsonist that is competitive when it SELLS must pass the lower cost on. One with power on both sides keeps it, and consumers see nothing.

realExample.text: A single dairy processor buying from many small farms sets what it pays; whether shoppers see a lower price depends on whether it faces competition when it sells.

sections.misconception: Students conclude that a minimum wage always reduces employment. In a competitive market a floor above equilibrium does; in a monopsonised one a floor between the two wages RAISES employment, because the firm already employs below the competitive level.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 says Examine requires evaluation and a brief assessment of the arguments as well as a chain of reasoning. The assessment here turns on one question: does the buyer face competition when it sells? Everything for consumers follows from that.

recall.prompt: Work the three gaps out from the two outcomes: 18 workers at $65 under monopsony, 24 at $80 competitively, with the last worker adding $110:
template: Jobs forgone: 24 − 18 = ___ workers
Wage forgone a worker: $80 − $65 = ___
And what the last worker adds against what she is paid: $110 − $65 = ___
hints: subtract the two employment figures
subtract the two wages
subtract the wage from the marginal revenue product

sections.title: Characteristics of a Contestable Market
sections.keyIdea: A market is contestable when outsiders could enter easily and leave without loss, so the THREAT of entry disciplines the firms inside it.

body.text: Everything so far has counted the firms IN a market. **Contestability** is about the firms outside it.
A market is **contestable** when entry is easy and — the part students leave out — **exit is easy too**. Its characteristics:

items: **Low barriers to entry** — nothing legal, technical or financial stops a new firm from beginning to trade.
**Low barriers to exit** — a firm that enters and does badly can leave without losing what it spent getting in.
**Low sunk costs** — the assets can be sold or used in another market, so entering is not a one-way bet.
**Equal access to technology** — an entrant can obtain the same methods and the same inputs as the firms already there.
**Perfect information** — potential entrants can see that the incumbents are earning more than normal profit.

body.text: What makes this a separate theory is that **the threat of entry is enough**. A market with two firms may behave competitively if a third could enter next month, because both know that any price worth entering for will attract entry. No third firm need exist.

So contestability is a **spectrum, not a structure**. A market can hold one firm and be highly contestable, or a dozen and — if entry is blocked and exit costly — barely contestable. It asks a different question from the four chapters before it.

realExample.text: Road haulage on a route may have two firms and be priced as if it had ten, because a haulier elsewhere can put lorries on it within a week and take them off again.

sections.misconception: Students define a contestable market by low barriers to ENTRY and stop. Exit matters as much: a firm that cannot leave without loss hesitates to enter.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Define as requiring the meaning of a term, concept or phrase. A contestable market is one where the threat of entry constrains incumbents — which needs entry AND exit to be easy, two conditions and not one.

recall.prompt: Sort each statement by whether it is a characteristic of a contestable market:

groups.name: Makes a market MORE contestable
items: A licence is not needed and the depot can be rented by the month
The lorries have a resale market if the route disappoints
Any operator can buy the same vehicles and the same software
groups.why: Contestability is about whether entry and exit are cheap: no licence to obtain, a depot that can be given up, assets with a resale market and methods anyone can buy.

groups.name: Says nothing about contestability
items: There are already nine firms trading in the market
Every firm sells an identical tonne-kilometre
The incumbents are currently earning unusually well
None of the incumbents is currently earning much
groups.why: Everything here is about the firms INSIDE the market. Their number, their product and how much they are earning are separate questions — profit is what TRIGGERS entry into a contestable market, not what makes it contestable.

sections.title: The Significance of Sunk Costs
sections.keyIdea: Sunk costs are what make entry irreversible, so they determine contestability more directly than the cost of entering does.

body.text: Sunk costs get their own requirement here, having already appeared among chapter 4's barriers, because for contestability they are not one barrier among six but the decisive one.

A firm thinking of entering asks not what entry costs but what it costs **if it goes wrong**. Where the assets can be sold or redeployed, a failed entry costs the difference between what was paid and what is recovered. Where they cannot, it costs everything.

So sunk costs turn a reversible experiment into a commitment, which changes who will try. A market can have low entry costs in total and be uncontestable if all of them are sunk — an advertising-intensive market is the standard case, since a campaign has no resale value.

The mirror is **hit-and-run entry**. A firm enters while incumbents' profit is above normal, takes some, and leaves when it is competed away, carrying its assets on. It is only possible where sunk costs are low, and its mere possibility holds the incumbents' price down.

Incumbents know this, which is why some create sunk costs deliberately: heavy brand spending, capacity ahead of demand and long exclusive contracts all raise what an entrant must commit and cannot recover.

realExample.text: An aircraft is among the least sunk of large assets: it can be flown to another route, leased out or sold into a world market. A tunnel under a strait is among the most sunk, and nobody enters that market speculatively.

sections.misconception: Students equate high entry costs with low contestability. The question is what share of the cost is recoverable: a market needing a large fleet of standard vehicles can be highly contestable, while one needing a modest but entirely sunk marketing spend may not be.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 says Discuss requires the validity and significance of arguments to be considered with reference to context. Sunk costs are context-dependent by nature — the same asset is sunk in one market and not another — so name the context.

recall.prompt: Two firms each spend $500,000 to enter. One buys aircraft; the other bores a tunnel. Complete the comparison:
template: The aircraft can be sold or flown elsewhere, so most of that spending is ___
The tunnel cannot be moved and has no other use, so all of it is ___
Only the first firm can enter, take the excess profit and leave again, which is called ___ entry
hints: what an asset with a resale market makes the spending
the word for spending that cannot come back
the name for entering and leaving again

sections.title: Implications for Profitability and Pricing
sections.keyIdea: In a contestable market incumbents hold profit near the normal level and price low enough to make entry unattractive, because the alternative is to invite it.

body.text: The specification names two things contestability changes: **profitability** and **pricing decisions**.

**Profitability.** Supernormal profit here is a signal visible to everybody outside, and acting on it is cheap. So incumbents cannot hold profit above the normal level for long: either entry competes it away, or they keep it low enough that entry is not worth attempting. Either way, **profit tends to normal even with very few firms.**

**Pricing: limit pricing again, for a different reason.** In chapter 4 an oligopolist priced below an entrant's average cost to protect a position built on scale. Here the same tool answers a different threat: price low enough that entering is not worth the trouble, accepting a smaller margin than market share would allow.

Two more follow. Incumbents keep **costs down**, since a firm carrying X-inefficiency cannot also hold a low limit price — pressure the number of firms would not predict. And they may build **strategic barriers**: brand spending, capacity ahead of demand, exclusive contracts, all raising an entrant's sunk costs.
Hence the lesson this chapter exists for: **market structure is not conduct.** A concentration ratio counts who is inside; contestability asks who could come in.

realExample.text: A city with two accountancy practices may see fees held down by how easily a third could open. A regulator counting practices would see a problem that is not there.

sections.misconception: Students conclude that a contestable market produces the perfectly competitive outcome. It pushes price and profit towards competitive levels without the many firms or the identical product, and it does so through a threat rather than through rivalry — so allocative efficiency is approached and not guaranteed.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 says Evaluate requires multi-stage chains of reasoning with reference to context and a critical assessment so that informed judgements may be made. A judgement about a concentrated market needs the contestability question asked as well as the structure described.

recall.prompt: Put these in the order in which they happen as the threat of entry disciplines an incumbent:
correctOrder: Suppose an incumbent in a market with low sunk costs raises its price above the normal level
Firms outside can see that profit, and low barriers make entering cheap
Because exit is easy too, entering is a reversible experiment rather than a commitment
Somebody enters, takes the profitable business and leaves again once the excess profit has gone
Foreseeing all of it, the incumbent never raises the price at all: it holds a limit price of $28
why: The chain begins with a SUPPOSITION, because the sequence is what the incumbent foresees rather than what it does.
Seeing the profit and being able to act on it are two separate conditions, and both are needed next.
Easy EXIT is what makes entry worth attempting, and it is the condition students leave out.
Entry removes the profit, and the departure is what makes it hit-and-run — which needs the low sunk costs of step three.
The incumbent’s low price is the CONSEQUENCE of the whole sequence being foreseeable, so it comes last.

sections.title: Costs and Benefits of Contestability
sections.keyIdea: Consumers gain lower prices and pressure on costs; firms lose the security that funds long-term investment, and the discipline can be undone by incumbents raising sunk costs.

body.text: Costs and benefits to **firms and consumers** — monopoly's pair, with nearly the opposite answers.

**Consumers gain.** Prices sit closer to cost, so allocative inefficiency is smaller than the number of firms suggests; incumbents are pushed to remove X-inefficiency; and the market stays open to a firm with a better idea.

**And bear a cost, the dynamic one.** A firm that cannot hold supernormal profit has less to invest and less certainty of recovering a long investment, so where the improvement consumers want needs patient spending — a network, a research programme — contestability works against them. Hit-and-run entry has its own cost: a firm that takes the profitable business and leaves is not there when the market is thin.

**For firms** the cost is security: profit is harder to hold and costs must stay at their minimum permanently rather than when challenged. Against that, a contestable market is one a firm can ENTER, so what threatens an incumbent is every outsider's opportunity.

**And the discipline is not self-sustaining.** All of it depends on sunk costs staying low, and incumbents can raise them deliberately. A market that was contestable can be made less so, which is why competition authorities watch conduct that raises entry costs and not only prices.

realExample.text: A market served by firms that enter and leave cheaply gets keen prices and little long-horizon investment. The infrastructure it runs on is usually built by somebody protected.

sections.misconception: Students treat contestability as unambiguously good because it lowers prices. Its weakness is the same as perfect competition's — profit near the normal level leaves little to invest — and it can be dismantled by the incumbents it was disciplining.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 says Evaluate requires the validity and significance of arguments and concepts to be considered and a critical assessment of the evidence. The significant qualification here is that contestability depends on a condition — low sunk costs — that firms in the market can change.

recall.prompt: Match each party to what contestability does to it:

pairs.right: Prices closer to cost, and pressure on incumbents to remove waste
pairs.why: The threat of entry pushes price towards cost and leaves no room for X-inefficiency, which is the case for contestability.

pairs.right: Less patient investment, because supernormal profit cannot be held
pairs.why: The same mechanism removes the profit that funds a network or a research programme, which is the case against it.

pairs.right: Lose the security that lets them plan, and must hold costs at the minimum permanently
pairs.why: Profit is harder to hold and the pressure on cost never lets up, whether or not an entrant ever appears.

pairs.right: Gain the opportunity that the same conditions create
pairs.why: What threatens an incumbent is an opportunity from the other side, which is why the same conditions cut both ways.

takeaway: One buyer: supply is the AVERAGE cost of the input, so marginal cost rises twice as fast.
18 at $65 against 24 at $80: a floor between them raises BOTH.
Contestability needs easy entry AND easy exit. The THREAT is enough; no entrant need appear.
Sunk costs turn a reversible experiment into a commitment. Hit-and-run entry needs them low.
So profit tends to normal and price to a limit price. Structure is not conduct.
And the discipline is not self-sustaining: incumbents can raise sunk costs deliberately.

notes.title: Efficiency and Concentration
notes.keyIdea: The four concepts of efficiency, and how a concentration ratio is calculated and read.

items.text: Allocative efficiency — reached where P = MC: the last unit is worth exactly what it cost to make.
Productive efficiency — producing at the lowest attainable average cost, the bottom of the AC curve.
Dynamic efficiency — investment and innovation lowering costs or improving the product over time.
X-inefficiency — costs ABOVE the lowest attainable level for the output chosen.
n-firm concentration ratio — the combined market share of the largest n firms.
MC cuts AC at AC's minimum, so MC = AC identifies the productively efficient output: $28 at 6 crates.
P > MC means too little is produced; P < MC means too much. The gap is the measure of allocative inefficiency.
Two markets can share a CR5 of 80% and have CR3s of 64% and 49%: the ratio hides the SHAPE of the market, and says nothing about conduct or contestability.

takeaway: Allocative is about the MIX (P = MC); productive is about the COST (lowest AC).
X-inefficiency is above the curve; productive inefficiency is the wrong point on it.
Quote n with every concentration ratio, and use it to identify a structure, not to judge conduct.

notes.title: Perfect Competition
notes.keyIdea: The benchmark structure: assumptions, both equilibria, the shutdown point and the efficiency verdict.

items.text: Perfect competition — many small firms, a homogeneous product, free entry and exit, perfect information.
Normal profit — the return that keeps resources in the industry; already inside the AC curve.
Shutdown point — the minimum of average variable cost: the price at which producing and stopping lose the same.
The firm faces a HORIZONTAL demand curve at the market price, so AR = MR = P and MR = MC becomes P = MC.
Short run at $72: output 8 crates, AC $33, profit $312.
Entry raises supply and lowers price until P = lowest AC = $28 at 6 crates: P = MR = MC = AC, profit $0.
Short run: produce while P ≥ AVC. At $15 the loss is −$72 — exactly the fixed cost — and the contribution is $0.
Long run: allocatively and productively efficient; dynamically the weakest, because normal profit funds nothing and perfect information rewards nobody.

takeaway: The firm’s demand curve is horizontal; the MARKET demand curve still slopes down.
Long-run signature: P = MR = MC = AC at the bottom of AC, $28.
Shut down below min AVC, not below min AC: the fixed cost is owed either way.

notes.title: Monopolistic Competition
notes.keyIdea: Many firms and free entry with a differentiated product, and the long-run tangency that follows.

items.text: Monopolistic competition — many firms, free entry, a DIFFERENTIATED product, independent decisions.
Product differentiation — buyers seeing firms’ products as different: physical, marketing or distribution.
Excess capacity — the gap between the long-run output and the lowest-cost output: 2 crates here.
Differentiation makes the firm’s demand curve slope DOWN, and close substitutes keep it highly elastic.
Short run: MR = MC at 5 crates; price off AR at $47.50; AC $29.40; profit $90.50.
Entry by close substitutes shifts AR LEFT and flattens it until AR is TANGENT to AC: 4 crates at $34 = AC, profit $0.
Tangency implies MR = MC there as well: MR $8 = MC $8 at 4 crates.

A downward-sloping AR can only touch a U-shaped AC where AC is FALLING, so the tangency is left of the minimum: neither productive ($34 against $28) nor allocative (P $34 against MC $8) efficiency holds.

takeaway: One assumption changed from perfect competition: the product is differentiated.
The long-run tangency is on the FALLING part of AC, never at its minimum.
Excess capacity and P > MC are the price of variety, not evidence of failure.

notes.title: Oligopoly: Barriers to Entry and Exit
notes.keyIdea: What oligopoly assumes, and the six barriers that keep the few firms few.

items.text: Oligopoly — a few firms dominate; each firm’s best decision depends on the others’. Products may be identical or differentiated.
Interdependence — a firm must anticipate rivals’ responses before it can choose its own price or output.
Sunk cost — spending that cannot be recovered on leaving the market.
Limit pricing — a price below an ENTRANT's average cost and above the incumbent's: $28 against $32 and $20.
The six barriers (spec order): economies of scale, limit pricing, patents, branding, sunk costs, legal.
Scale and limit pricing together: the incumbent earns $8 a unit while an entrant would lose $4.
Patents make the METHOD unavailable, branding makes CUSTOMERS expensive, legal barriers make PERMISSION unavailable.
Sunk costs are a barrier to EXIT and therefore to ENTRY: the test is what share of the entry cost is recoverable, not how large it is.

takeaway: Interdependence, not the number of firms, is what makes oligopoly different.
A limit price is profitable for the incumbent. That is what separates it from predatory pricing.
A large recoverable entry cost is a weaker barrier than a small sunk one.

notes.title: Oligopoly: Interdependence and Collusion
notes.keyIdea: Interdependence, the two-firm game, and how collusion works and fails.

items.text: Collusive behaviour — firms acting together on price or output, by agreement (overt) or without one (tacit).
Cartel — a formal agreement to fix price, restrict output or divide a market. Illegal in most jurisdictions.
Price leadership — one firm moves its price and the others follow, with no agreement.
Dominant strategy — a choice that is best whatever the other firm does.
The two-firm game, $m a year: both hold 50/50; one cuts 70/20; both cut 30/30.
Cutting beats holding against EITHER choice by the rival (70 > 50, and 30 > 20), so both cut and both do worse by 40 between them.
Collusion holds with few firms, similar costs, stable demand, detectable cheating, a standardised product.
It fails as those reverse, and because breaking an agreement while the other keeps it pays 20 more.
Collusion’s four stakeholder groups are PRODUCERS, CONSUMERS, WORKERS and GOVERNMENTS — each with a cost and a benefit.

takeaway: The equilibrium is the best each can do given the other, not the best for both.
Overt collusion can be prosecuted; tacit price leadership leaves nothing to find.
Whether collusion HOLDS turns on detection, not on intention.

notes.title: Oligopoly: Price and Non-Price Competition
notes.keyIdea: The three forms of price competition, the five of non-price competition, and who gains from each.

items.text: Price war — a sequence of matched price cuts, leaving every firm selling lower than it wanted.
Predatory pricing — a price below the SELLER's own average variable cost, to remove a rival: $14 against an AVC of $16.
Non-price competition — winning customers by any means other than lowering price.
Price competition: price wars, predatory pricing, limit pricing. Non-price: advertising and branding, quality, endorsement, product placement, after-sales service.
The test that separates the two low prices: predatory is below the SELLER's AVC and loses $2 a unit; limit pricing is below an ENTRANT's AC and earns $8.
Firms prefer non-price competition because a price cut is matched within days and a reputation takes rivals years to copy — and it makes demand less elastic.
Costs and benefits run to FIRMS, CONSUMERS, EMPLOYEES and SUPPLIERS, and the two kinds of competition pull employees and suppliers in opposite directions.

takeaway: Name the cost the price is being compared with: the seller’s AVC, or an entrant’s AC.
All five forms of non-price competition, including endorsement, product placement and after-sales service.
A price war can end with one fewer firm and a higher price than it started at.

notes.title: Monopoly
notes.keyIdea: The monopoly equilibrium and its welfare loss, natural monopoly, price discrimination, and all three efficiency tests.

items.text: Monopoly — one seller, no close substitute, high barriers to entry and exit.
Natural monopoly — average cost falling across the whole range of market demand, so one firm supplies more cheaply than several.
Third-degree price discrimination — different prices to different GROUPS for the same product, not reflecting a cost difference.
Welfare loss — the area between demand and MC over the output a monopolist withholds.
P = 120 − 4Q so MR = 120 − 8Q; MR = MC = $24 gives Q = 12 megalitres; price off AR = $72; profit $576.
Competitive comparison: P = MC = $24, Q = 24. So 12 megalitres withheld, and DWL = ½ × 12 × $48 = $288.
Natural monopoly: AC = $2 + $9,000 ÷ Q. One firm at 1,000 costs $11 a unit; two at 500 cost $20. Regulate rather than split.
Price discrimination needs market power, separable groups with different elasticities, and no resale. Market A (|PED| 1.50) pays $72; Market B (|PED| 2.00) pays $48.
Allocative: fails, necessarily, since MR < AR. Productive: no pressure towards it, and X-inefficiency is likely. Dynamic: may be funded by the supernormal profit.

takeaway: The price comes off AR above the MR = MC output, never off MR.
The welfare loss is a triangle and it has an area: $288 here.
A natural monopoly should be regulated, not broken up. The less elastic market pays the higher price.

notes.title: Monopsony and Contestability
notes.keyIdea: The single buyer, and why the threat of entry can discipline a market with few firms in it.

items.text: Monopsony — a single buyer of a good or of labour, facing many sellers who cannot go elsewhere.
Contestable market — one in which the THREAT of entry constrains incumbents: easy entry AND easy exit, low sunk costs.
Hit-and-run entry — entering while profit is above normal and leaving when it is competed away.
A single buyer must raise the price for EVERY unit to get one more, so the marginal cost of the input rises twice as fast as supply: w = $20 + 2.5L and MCL = $20 + 5L.
MCL = MRP gives 18 workers; the wage comes off SUPPLY at $65. Competitively: 24 at $80 — 6 more jobs and $15 more a worker.
The last worker adds $110 and is paid $65: a gap of $45. A minimum wage between $65 and $80 raises wage AND employment.
Contestability: profit tends to normal and price towards a limit price, however few firms are in the market, because supernormal profit invites entry.
It all depends on SUNK COSTS staying low — and incumbents can raise them deliberately through brand spending, capacity ahead of demand or exclusive contracts.

takeaway: Read the monopsony wage off the SUPPLY curve, not off MCL.
Contestability needs easy exit as well as easy entry. The threat is enough.
Structure is not conduct: count who could enter, not only who is in.

quiz.question: Allocative efficiency is reached at the output where:
options: average cost is at its lowest
the firm earns the largest possible profit
price equals marginal cost
marginal revenue equals zero
quiz.explanation: Price measures the value of the last unit to the buyer and marginal cost measures what the resources used on it would otherwise have produced, so P = MC is the condition for the last unit to be worth exactly what it cost. Producing at the lowest average cost is PRODUCTIVE efficiency, which is a different test.

quiz.question: A firm is described as X-inefficient. This means that:
options: it is producing at an output where average cost is not at its minimum
its costs are above the lowest attainable level for the output it produces
it is charging a price above its marginal cost
it has chosen not to invest in the newer technology that its rivals have adopted
quiz.explanation: X-inefficiency puts the firm ABOVE its own average cost curve — waste at whatever output has been chosen. Producing at the wrong output is productive inefficiency, which leaves the firm on the curve at the wrong point; charging above marginal cost is allocative inefficiency.

quiz.question: Five firms in a market hold 28%, 22%, 14%, 9%, 7%. The three-firm concentration ratio is:
quiz.explanation: An n-firm concentration ratio adds the market shares of the largest n firms: 28% + 22% + 14% = 64%. Adding the next two firms gives the FIVE-firm ratio of 80%, and 21.3% is the average of the three shares rather than their total.

quiz.question: Which kind of efficiency cannot be shown as a point on a single static diagram?
options: Dynamic efficiency
Allocative efficiency
Productive efficiency
None of them — all three can be marked on one diagram
quiz.explanation: Dynamic efficiency is a claim about how the cost curves MOVE over time as a firm invests and innovates, so it cannot be a point on a diagram drawn at one moment. Allocative efficiency is marked where price meets marginal cost and productive efficiency at the bottom of the average cost curve.

quiz.question: A firm could produce at an average cost of $28 and is actually producing at the same output for $32. The $4 difference is:
options: X-inefficiency
productive inefficiency
allocative inefficiency
a diseconomy of scale
quiz.explanation: The output has not changed, so the firm has not chosen the wrong point on its cost curve — it is sitting ABOVE the curve, which is X-inefficiency. A diseconomy of scale would raise the curve itself as the firm grew, and allocative inefficiency is about the gap between price and marginal cost.

quiz.question: Two markets both have a five-firm concentration ratio of 80%. It follows that:
options: they may still have very different three-firm ratios and behave differently
the largest firm in each has the same market share
both markets are oligopolies with identical conduct
neither of the two markets could be contestable, because both are concentrated
quiz.explanation: A five-firm ratio is one number and many shapes produce it: 64% plus two small firms, or five near-equals with a three-firm ratio of 49%. The ratio counts who holds the market, so it cannot say what the largest firm holds, how the firms behave, or whether a firm outside could enter.

quiz.question: Which of these makes a market structure likely to deliver productive efficiency?
options: A high concentration ratio, because large firms have lower costs
High barriers to entry, because the firm can plan for the long term
A differentiated product, because a firm able to charge more can cover its costs more easily
Free entry combined with an identical product, so a firm with higher costs is undercut
quiz.explanation: Pressure is what delivers productive efficiency: where entry is free and the product identical, a firm that lets costs drift is undercut and loses everything. Large scale can lower costs without forcing a firm to reach the lowest attainable one, and barriers remove the pressure rather than adding to it.

quiz.question: A perfectly competitive firm faces a horizontal demand curve because:
options: the market demand curve for this product is itself horizontal at the going price
its product is identical to every other firm’s and it is too small to affect the market price
it has agreed with its rivals to charge the same price as all of them
buyers have no information at all about the alternative suppliers
quiz.explanation: A homogeneous product means a firm asking more sells nothing, and being small means it can sell its whole output at the going price — so the line it faces is horizontal at that price. The MARKET demand curve still slopes downward; the two curves are different things.

quiz.question: Mwangi Orchards faces a market price of $72 a crate. Its marginal cost reaches $72 at 8 crates a day and its average cost there is $33. Its profit is:
quiz.explanation: Profit is the margin a crate multiplied by the output: ($72 − $33) × 8 = $312. $576 is total revenue before any cost is taken off, and $39 is the margin on one crate rather than the total.

quiz.question: In long-run equilibrium under perfect competition:
options: price is equal to marginal cost and remains above average cost at that output
average cost has reached its minimum and price is still above it
marginal revenue has fallen to zero at the chosen output
price, marginal revenue, marginal cost and average cost are all equal at the minimum of average cost
quiz.explanation: Entry continues while supernormal profit remains, so it stops only where price has been driven to the lowest average cost — and at the bottom of the average cost curve marginal cost equals average cost as well. For Mwangi Orchards that is $28 at 6 crates, with all four measures equal.

quiz.question: A firm's minimum average variable cost is $15 and its minimum average cost is $28. At a price of $20 in the short run it should:
options: shut down, because the price is below average cost and it is making a loss
shut down, because the price is below the long-run break-even price
keep producing, because the price is above the level at which it would earn supernormal profit
keep producing, because the price covers its variable cost and contributes to the fixed cost
quiz.explanation: At $20 the firm is making a loss, since the price is below average cost. But the fixed cost is owed whether it produces or not, so the comparison that matters is with average VARIABLE cost of $15: above that, every crate leaves something towards the fixed cost, so producing loses less than stopping.

quiz.question: Why is perfect competition usually judged the weakest of the four structures on dynamic efficiency?
options: Firms are too small to understand new technology
Consumers in such markets do not want improved products
Marginal cost is above average cost at the equilibrium output
Firms earn only normal profit in the long run, so there is no surplus to fund research
quiz.explanation: A structure whose long-run equilibrium leaves nothing above the normal return has nothing to invest, and perfect information means any improvement is available to every rival at once, so nothing is captured by whoever made it. The incentive to ADOPT a cost-lowering method remains strong, which is a different thing.

quiz.question: Monopolistic competition differs from perfect competition in exactly one assumption. That assumption is:
options: the product is differentiated rather than identical
there are few firms rather than many
entry to the market is blocked by barriers that the incumbent firms control
firms do not aim to maximise profit
quiz.explanation: Many firms, free entry and profit maximisation are all carried over unchanged. Differentiation is the single change, and it is enough to tilt the firm’s demand curve downward, which is what alters every result that follows.

quiz.question: A shop sells a bag of rice identical to the one next door but offers free delivery. This is:
options: physical differentiation
marketing differentiation
distribution differentiation
not differentiation, because the product is identical
quiz.explanation: Where and how a product can be bought is part of what the buyer is choosing, which is distribution differentiation — and it works precisely because the product itself is unchanged. Physical differentiation would alter the rice; marketing differentiation would alter the name or the packaging.

quiz.question: Nile Crafts maximises profit where MR = MC at 5 crates a day, facing the demand curve P = 80 − 6.5Q. The price it charges is:
quiz.explanation: The price is read off the DEMAND curve at the profit-maximising output: 80 − 6.5 × 5 = $47.50. Reading it off the marginal revenue curve instead gives $15, which is the commonest error here; $29.40 is average cost at that output.

quiz.question: In long-run equilibrium a monopolistically competitive firm’s demand curve is tangent to its average cost curve:
options: exactly at the minimum point of the average cost curve
on the falling part of the average cost curve, to the left of its minimum
on the rising part of the curve, to the right of its minimum
at the output where marginal cost reaches its own lowest point
quiz.explanation: A downward-sloping straight line can only touch a U-shaped curve where that curve is also sloping down, so the tangency is necessarily left of the minimum. For Nile Crafts it is 4 crates against a lowest-cost output of 6, and the gap of 2 is the excess capacity.

quiz.question: Excess capacity in monopolistic competition means that:
options: the firm has bought machinery and floor space that it has never once put to any use
the firm produces less than the output at which its average cost would be lowest
the firm could sell more at the current price but chooses not to
average cost is above marginal cost at every output
quiz.explanation: It is the gap between the long-run output and the productively efficient output — 2 crates for Nile Crafts — and it follows from where the tangency falls rather than from any management decision. What consumers get in exchange is variety.

quiz.question: What distinguishes oligopoly from the other three market structures?
options: It always contains exactly three or four competing firms
Its firms always end up charging one another’s prices, whatever their own costs are
Its product is always identical from one firm to the next
Each firm’s best decision depends on what it expects named rivals to do
quiz.explanation: Interdependence is the defining feature: a perfectly competitive firm has too many rivals to plan around any one of them, a monopoly has none, and a monopolistically competitive firm plans around none in particular. There is no fixed number of firms, and the product may be identical or differentiated.

quiz.question: An incumbent's average cost is $20 a unit and an entrant would face $32. Setting a price of $28 is an example of:
options: predatory pricing
price leadership
a price war
limit pricing
quiz.explanation: The price is below the average cost an ENTRANT would face and above the incumbent's own, so the incumbent still earns $8 a unit while entry cannot pay — which is limit pricing. A predatory price would be below the incumbent's own average variable cost and would lose it money.

quiz.question: Which barrier to entry has a fixed expiry date built into it?
options: Economies of scale
Sunk costs
Branding
A patent
quiz.explanation: A patent confers an exclusive right for a defined period, after which the method becomes available to anyone and the barrier disappears. The other three last as long as the technology, the nature of the assets or the brand itself does.

quiz.question: A firm considering entry finds that the equipment it would need can be sold on easily in a world market. This means that:
options: the entry cost is high, so the market is harder to contest
there are no barriers to entry of any kind in this market
the entry cost is largely not sunk, so the market is easier to contest
economies of scale must be absent from this industry
quiz.explanation: What matters is how much of the entry cost could be recovered on the way out, not how large it is: equipment with a resale market makes entry a reversible experiment rather than a commitment. Other barriers may still be present, and scale economies are a separate question.

quiz.question: Two firms choose between holding and cutting price. Holding pays each 50; the firm that cuts alone gets 70 while the other gets 20; both cutting pays each 30. Cutting is:
options: the best choice only if the rival holds its price
the best choice only if the rival also cuts
a dominant strategy for both firms
never worth doing for either firm
quiz.explanation: Check each of the rival's choices in turn. If the rival holds, cutting pays 70 against 50; if the rival cuts, cutting pays 30 against 20. Better in both cases makes it dominant — and both firms reasoning this way end at 30 each, 40 worse between them than holding.

quiz.question: In the equilibrium of that game both firms cut their price. The outcome is:
options: the best each firm can do given what the other is doing, and worse for both than cooperating
the best available outcome for both firms
unstable, because either firm could improve by raising its price alone
impossible, because both firms would rather cooperate
quiz.explanation: Neither firm can improve by changing its own choice alone, which is what makes it an equilibrium — but both holding would have paid each of them 50 rather than 30. Wanting to cooperate is not enough when cutting pays better whatever the other does.

quiz.question: Which condition makes a collusive agreement HARDER to sustain?
options: A small number of firms in the market
Published prices that every firm can check
Discounts negotiated privately with individual buyers
Costs that are similar across the firms
quiz.explanation: Collusion survives on detection: a discount nobody else can see cannot be punished, so the temptation to cheat goes unchecked. Few firms, visible prices and similar costs all make an agreement easier to reach and easier to police.

quiz.question: Prices in a market move together, but investigators find no agreement of any kind between the firms. This is consistent with:
options: an illegal cartel that has covered its tracks
perfect competition, in which all firms charge the same price
predatory pricing by the largest firm
tacit collusion through price leadership
quiz.explanation: Price leadership needs no communication: one firm moves and each of the others follows because following is what is best for it, so prices move together with nothing to find. That is exactly why parallel pricing is not by itself evidence of an agreement.

quiz.question: A firm whose average variable cost is $16 a unit sells at $14, intending to raise the price once a rival has left. This is:
options: limit pricing
predatory pricing
non-price competition
productive efficiency
quiz.explanation: The price is below the SELLER's own average variable cost, so it loses $2 a unit on the variable costs alone — a deliberate loss no firm would accept except for what it does to a rival. A limit price stays above the seller's own cost and is profitable throughout.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT one of the five forms of non-price competition the specification names?
options: Endorsement
Product placement
Limit pricing
After-sales service
quiz.explanation: The five are advertising and branding, quality, endorsement, product placement and after-sales service. Limit pricing is a form of PRICE competition — it works by setting a price below the level at which entry would pay.

quiz.question: Why do oligopolists often prefer non-price competition to cutting price?
options: A price cut is matched within days, while a reputation takes rivals years to copy
Non-price competition is cheaper than a price cut
Competition law prohibits changing prices in a concentrated market
A price cut cannot increase the quantity a firm sells
quiz.explanation: Interdependence is the reason: a visible price cut is matched and leaves everybody with the same customers and less money, while quality, a service network or a trusted name gives an advantage that lasts and makes demand less elastic. Advertising budgets are often larger than the price cut would have cost.

quiz.question: A price war ends when one of the firms leaves the market. For consumers the likely long-run result is:
options: a permanently lower price, since the surviving firm has proved it can supply cheaply
no change at all, because the remaining firms still compete
a more concentrated market, in which the price may settle above where it started
lower quality but the same price as before the war
quiz.explanation: The gain to consumers lasts while the war does. A firm leaving removes a competitor, so the market is more concentrated afterwards and the survivor faces less pressure — which is why a war that removes a rival can end with a higher price than the one it began at.

quiz.question: A monopolist faces P = 120 − 4Q with a constant marginal cost of $24. Its profit-maximising output is:
options: 12 megalitres
24 megalitres
30 megalitres
15 megalitres
quiz.explanation: Marginal revenue is 120 − 8Q, so MR = MC gives 120 − 8Q = 24 and Q = 12. Setting the DEMAND curve equal to marginal cost instead gives 24, which is the competitive output, and 15 is where marginal revenue reaches zero.

quiz.question: That monopolist produces 12 megalitres and charges $72. A competitive industry with the same costs would produce 24 at $24. The welfare loss is:
quiz.explanation: The loss is the triangle between the demand curve and marginal cost over the output withheld: ½ × 12 × $48 = $288. $576 is the monopolist's profit, which is TRANSFERRED from consumers rather than lost, and $48 is the gap between price and marginal cost on one megalitre.

quiz.question: A market is a natural monopoly when:
options: long-run average cost is still falling at an output as large as the whole market
one firm has been granted a legal monopoly by the state
the firm is very large compared with others in the economy
the product has no close substitute available at any price that a buyer might be offered
quiz.explanation: The test is where minimum efficient scale falls relative to market size: if average cost is still falling at the size of the whole market, splitting output between firms raises the cost of supply. A network costing $9,000 a day plus $2 a unit gives $11 for one firm serving 1,000 units and $20 for two serving half each.

quiz.question: Third-degree price discrimination requires that the groups charged different prices:
options: cannot resell to each other and differ in their price elasticity of demand
face different costs of supply from the seller
are of roughly similar size to one another in the seller’s principal market
both have inelastic demand for the product
quiz.explanation: Different elasticities are what make two prices more profitable than one, and no resale is what stops the two prices collapsing into one. A difference in the COST of supply would make the price difference something other than discrimination, and if both groups had inelastic demand there would be no reason to charge either of them less.

quiz.question: A monopolist sells in two separable markets at the same marginal cost. Market A has an elasticity of demand of −1.50 and market B −2.00. The firm will charge:
options: the higher price in market B, where demand is more elastic
the higher price in market A, where demand is less elastic
the same price in both, since marginal cost is the same
a price below marginal cost in market B to build its share
quiz.explanation: The less elastic market is the one whose buyers will not switch, so it bears the higher price: $72 against $48 here. The identical marginal cost is exactly why the price difference is discrimination rather than a difference in cost.

quiz.question: The supply of labour to a monopsonist is w = $20 + 2.5L. Its marginal cost of labour is:
quiz.explanation: To hire one more worker the single buyer must raise the wage for EVERY worker it already employs, not only the last, so the marginal cost of labour rises at twice the gradient of the supply curve. The supply curve itself is the AVERAGE cost of labour.

quiz.question: That monopsonist employs 18 workers, where the marginal cost of labour equals the marginal revenue product. The wage it pays is:
quiz.explanation: The wage is read off the SUPPLY curve at that employment level: $20 + 2.5 × 18 = $65. $110 is what the last worker adds and is what the marginal cost of labour has risen to; $80 is what a competitive market for the same labour would pay.

quiz.question: A minimum wage set between the monopsony wage and the competitive wage would:
options: raise the wage and lower the number employed
raise both the wage and the number employed
lower both the wage and the number employed
have no effect, because the firm is already at its profit-maximising employment
quiz.explanation: A monopsonist already employs below the competitive level — 18 against 24 here — because hiring one more raises the wage bill for everyone.
